subs.title: Conversational mock and notes on the weak answers

c.v: Set a timer for 45 minutes and answer out loud, as if the person asking sat across the table. No notes, no compiler and no going back to reread a page before you speak. There are ten questions below, each with one follow-up: twenty answers in all, so budget a little over two minutes for each, the time to read it, answer it and write its score down before moving to the next. Score each answer against the sentence that says what a strong answer contains: strong when every part of that sentence is there, partial when one part is missing or the words are close but not exact, weak when the mechanism is wrong or you reach for the page's exact example instead of explaining the idea in your own words.

Start with the ownership of a resource that a class hands out to the rest of a program, such as a socket a driver node opens once and reads from until shutdown. Ask yourself what makes a type its owner rather than a user of it, and answer, then ask what happens when a function copies that type without thinking. A strong answer says that the owner is the object whose destructor releases the resource, that the language runs that destructor on every way out of a scope, including an exception in flight, and that a naive copy duplicates the handle so two destructors release the same resource once each, which is a double free or a double close. A class has a hand-written destructor and nothing else. Ask what the compiler still generates for the other four special members, and why that is dangerous for a class holding a raw resource. A strong answer says the compiler still generates the copy constructor and copy assignment, member-wise, which for a raw pointer means copying the address, and it stops generating the two move operations, so an rvalue falls back to that same copying copy constructor. Ask what a comparator has to satisfy to be safe to hand to

A strong answer states the four rules of a strict weak ordering before anything else: irreflexive, an element is never less than itself; asymmetric, if a is less than b then b is never less than a; transitive for less than; and transitive for equivalence, where two elements are equivalent when neither is less than the other. Ask for the members of a bounded blocking queue with cancellation, named out loud, and why it needs two condition variables rather than one. A strong answer lists a mutex, one condition variable for producers waiting on room and one for consumers waiting on an item, the item container, the capacity and a closed flag, and explains that two condition variables give each one a single kind of waiter, which is what makes

An unseen link error names an undefined reference on one build and multiple definition on another. Ask what each one usually means. A strong answer says an undefined reference means a declaration exists but no translation unit defines that symbol, commonly a missing source file in the build or a forgotten library, while a multiple definition means the same non-inline symbol is defined in more than one translation unit that both end up in the same binary, commonly a function body sitting in a header without

. The follow-up: why can changing a struct's layout in a header break a program even though every file that includes it still compiles cleanly. A strong answer names the one-definition rule and the ABI: an object file compiled against the old layout and one compiled against the new layout disagree about member offsets and size, so linking them together, or loading one against a library built with the other, reads the wrong bytes at each offset without either compiler ever seeing an error. Take 15 minutes. Go down your list of scores and pull out every answer marked weak or partial. For each one, write three lines: the question, in your own words, the exact piece the strong answer needed that yours did not, and the single exercise you will redo closed book before the next mock, named by page and, where the page has more than one, by number, such as
, exercise 2. Do not write a line for an answer you scored strong: the point of this list is what to fix, not a record of everything you said.

Count your strong answers out of the twenty above. You pass this mock at 16 or more strong, with every weak answer carrying its one follow-up exercise. Fewer than 12 strong means going back through the sub-topics named above before the next attempt, not straight to a second mock: a conversational mock tests recall under a clock, and recall has nothing to draw on until the material is there to recall.
